Regular Council Meeting
CITY OF SOLANA BEACH
ACTION AGENDA
The Action Agenda of the City Council Meeting is a document provided immediately following the Council Meeting in order for staff and the public to be aware of the business transacted and actions taken by Council. This is a preliminary draft and not a public record. The meeting's legal record is the Minutes approved by the City Council.
Solana Beach City Council, Successor Agency to the Redevelopment Agency, Public Financing Authority, & Housing Authority
Joint REGULAR Meeting
Wednesday, April 25, 2012
6:00
P.M.
City Hall / Council Chambers
635 S. Highway 101, Solana Beach, California
Public Meeting Access
The Regular Meetings of the City Council are scheduled for the 2nd and 4th Wednesdays and are broadcast live on Cox Communications-Channel 19, Time Warner-Channel 24 (analog) or Channel 131 (digital) , and AT&T U-verse Channel 99. The video taping of meetings are maintained as a permanent record and contain a detailed account of the proceedings. Council meeting tapings are archived and available for viewing on the City's website.
Agenda Materials
A full City Council agenda packet including relative supporting documentation is available at City Hall, the Solana Beach Branch Library (157 Stevens Ave.), La Colonia Community Ctr., Fletcher Cove Lifeguard station, and online www.cityofsolanabeach.org. Agendas are posted at least 72 hours prior to the meeting. Writings and documents regarding an agenda of an open session meeting, received after the official posting, and distributed to the Council for consideration, will be made available for public viewing at the same time. In addition, items received at least 1 hour 30 minutes prior to the meeting time will be uploaded online with the courtesy agenda posting. Materials submitted for consideration should be forwarded to the City Clerk's department 858-720-2400. The designated location for viewing public documents is the City Clerk's office at City Hall during normal business hours.
Speakers
Please submit a speaker slip to the City Clerk prior to the meeting, or the announcement of the Section/Item, to provide public comment. Allotted times for speaking are outlined on the speaker's slip for each agenda section: Oral Communications, Consent, Public Hearings and Staff Reports.
American Disabilities Act Title 2
In compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, persons with a disability may request an agenda in appropriate alternative formats as required by Section 202. Any person with a disability who requires a modification or accommodation in order to participate in a meeting should direct such request to the City Clerk's office (858) 720-2400 at least 72 hours prior to the meeting.
As a courtesy to all meeting attendees, please set cellular phones and pagers to silent mode
and engage in conversations outside the Council Chambers.

B.1.
Adopt (1st Reading) Ordinance 435, Citywide Plastic Bag Use Reduction. (File 0230-55)
Recommendation: That the City Council
1.
Conduct the Public Hearing: Open the public hearing, Report Council disclosures, Receive public testimony, Close the public hearing.
2.
Introduce Ordinance 435 adding Municipal Code Chapter 5.01 related to plastic bag use reduction.
David Ott, City Manager, introduced the item. He stated Council directed Staff at the October 26, 2011 meeting to prepare a draft Ordinance which would 1) reduce point of sale distribution of use of single-use plastic bags by businesses in the City, 2) discourage the use of paper bags at the point of sale by requiring that retail businesses charge a 10 cent fee per bag, and 3) encourage the use of reusable bags by retail shoppers. He said that Council directed Staff to incorporate provisions of the ordinances of cities of Manhattan Beach, Long Beach, and Santa Monica into the City's ordinance and evaluate the potential for environmental effects associated with the adoption of the ordinance. He continued stating that City Staff prepared a draft ordinance in January 2012 with an initial CEQA study.
Leslea Meyerhoff, Consultant, presented a power point (on file) reviewing the draft ordinance and stated that the ordinance was based in part on the cities of Manhattan Beach, Long Beach, and Santa Monica, that the key provisions of the ordinance included, reducing the distribution and use of single-use plastic and paper bags, it would have a phased implementation, that it would prohibit the distribution of single-use bags, unless exemptions applied, a provision to allow distribution of recycled paper bags was included in the ordinance with a pass-through cost to the customer, that the City would not receive any funds from the pass-through fee, and that it did allow the use of product bags for the use of meat, produce, and other bulk goods.
Mayor Kellejian opened the public hearing.
Sarah Sheehy said she was was speaking on behalf of the California Grocers Association (CGA) and stated that they were very comfortable with the ordinance, that they appreciated the City moving forward with it, and that the language in the draft ordinance was confusing to retailers using recycled paper. She stated that the cities of Long Beach, Santa Monica, and Laguna Beach, had more clear language, that reusable bag use had increased to almost 98% within 6 months of implementation of ordinances in effect within other cities, that the City should amend the language to include that retails were "mandated" instead of "strongly encouraged" to provide incentives for reusable bag use, and that they would like to work with the City on the draft ordinance.
Chris Duggan said he was from the California Restaurant Association and stated that they appreciated the intent of the ordinance, that there were no exemptions for the health and safety of the dining public, that other cities had exemptions for restaurants because the removal of plastic bags in dining areas was a health concern, that bringing in reusable plastic bags was aconcern for cross contamination and public health and safety issue, and that they worked closely with all counties on this issue, and that additional fees for the use of bags charged to customers could hurt businesses in the current economic times.
Johanna Canlas, City Attorney, responded regarding the language in the proposed section that said "strongly encourage" was used to provide options for the retailer, that the retailer did not have to provide paper bags, that if they did provide paper bags charge no less than 10 cents per bag, which was a pass-through cost, and that the City would be enforcing the pass-through cost through the ordinance. She stated that the Health and Safety Code regulated health and sanitation standards for retail food facilities, there was litigation through the state regarding the pre-exemption of food facilities from plastic bags, and that there was language in the ordinance stating that it was not the City’s intent to preempt state regulations.
Jim Moriarti said he was CEO of Surfrider Foundation and stated that 44 California jurisdictions already had plastic bag ordinances, that the entire country of China implemented a similar law in 2008 and saved 1.6 milliontons of oil, that Honolulu had adopted an ordinance today, and that he supported the ordinance.
Peter Zahn stated that he was speaking on behalf of the U.S. Green Chamber of Commerce and that the ordinance was important and overdue, that there were no other cities in the county with it, the ordinance was fine as it was presented, that the 10 cent cost should be a minimum, and urged the Council to adopt the ordinance.
Johnny Pappas stated that he was a member of Surfrider Foundation and that he was a co-founder of the Rise Against Plastics which a local organization that had grown into an international effort to reduce the use of single-use plastics on the planet. He stated that he had sent an email to the Council about 2 years ago asking them to support a state-wide ordinance for a plastic bag ban, the bill failed and plastic bags were spoiling the land, clogged drains, ended up in the ocean and killed wildlife. He stated that Solana Beach was a smaller city within the county but had the ability to be a steward for the earth and the ocean.
Marilee McLean (time donated by Cheryl Aden) stated that there were many community members that supported the proposal and asked people in the audience to stand if they wanted to support the ordinance. She thanked those who already had adopted the habit of carrying reusable bags, that bags rolled across streets from dumpster into bushes and eventually ended up in gutters and the ocean, and that the City would be doing a small part to solve the problem. She said that some people were concerned about what to do with dog poop and how to line their trash cans, but that these were small problems with simple solutions, and that bits of plastic in every ocean was a big problem which demanded attention and action.
Jacy Bolden stated that she volunteered to coordinate a regional initiative called a "Day without a Bag," and thanked the City for long term efforts in making strides prior to this effort. She stated that the City was the first city to do proactive efforts to promote plastic bag recycling, and applauded Staff and residents for their involvement in a "Day without a Bag," a grassroots effort encouraging and educating about reusable plastic bags and that it was time for the City to take the next step.
Jack Hegenauer stated that he was speaking on behalf of the City’s Climate Action Advisory Team, known as Clean and Green, who had been working on the plastic bags for at least 5 years. He stated that the City would probably receive letters from the Plastic Bag Council, that their message was predictable to benefit a narrow sector of the economy by keeping American’s addiction to single-use plastic bags, that they were leaving an unsustainable mess for others to clean up, there were other sustainable solutions to pick-up dog poop, and that the plastic bag use reduction ordinance should be passed.
Connie Kortman said that she applauded the efforts, she was proud of the community, and that she would keep working on the task as long as it would take.
Belinda Smith stated that she was a member of Surfrider foundation and that they supported the City’s efforts to reduce litter in the environment, they recommended the 10 cent fee be required at all retailers, which would be in line with other ordinances, and that it would cause consumers to switch to reusable bags. She said she had a list of 44 cities in California that had similar ordinances, the City would set an example in the county, and that reusable bags in restaurants should not be an issue.
Walter Hicks asked everyone to make a conscious effort to look for plastic bags and that it would not take long, they were everywhere, and that there should be a yes vote.
Lane Sharman stated that he was with Clean and Green Committee and the Creation Care Committee of the Presbyterian Church. He said there were connected dots of climate change, plastic, and community choice aggregation, that some rights had greater consequences than the benefits, it was an inter-generational justice issue, and urged Council to be aggressive with the future. He stated that the City needed to lead and that a community choice aggregation was needed to have its own energy district, which was important for a clean energy future.
Steven Goetsch stated that he was the Chairman of the Clean and Green Committee and that the City was the first in the county to do this, that it was an interim solution to the problem, and that the ordinance was a better fix to the problem.
Roger Boyd read a letter by the City Council to Senator Wyland that was written several years ago, that urged the Senator’s support of Assembly Bill 1998 which would have banned plastic single-use carry out bags and regulated paper carryout bags at supermarkets, the bill was intended to reduce the adverse economical and environmental effects of plastic bag pollution. He stated that the state of California did not pass the legislation ban but the City might, that it was not about jobs and convenience but about the chemical industry that cared more about profits that family’s well being or the environment.
Mary Yang urged the Council to support the plastic bag reduction, that passing legislation in this area was not easy, and that the plastic bag manufactures were in a fight to save the industry. She stated that the industry was a 374 billion dollar industry in 2008, in California there were 6 on-going litigation cases against cities and counties trying to adopt similar ordinances, and that 5 of those litigations were brought on by Save the Plastic Bag Coalition. She stated that the City had received a comment from the Coalition, which contradicted all the facts and data on the topic, twelve cities and counties in California had succeeded in adopting bans that were already active, and that another 9 had adopted bans which would be active in the nearfuture.
Marty Benson stated that he was an "oilaholic," that he had been single-use plastic bag free for 5 years and had been car free for almost 2 years. He stated that a plastic bag was unnecessary and that this was the time to do it.
Jim Jaffee stated that was on the Advisory Committee for the Surfrider Foundation, that he became interested in plastic bags when Captain Charles Moore went to a Surfrider meeting and taught about the Pacific Gyre. He stated that plastic broke down to the size of plankton and was then eaten by fish, he had stopped using plastic bags, asked Council not to delay the ordinance, and to mitigate the impact by stopping the use of plastic bags.
MOTION: Moved by Heebner and seconded by Roberts to close the public hearing.
Motion carried unanimously.
Council discussion ensued regarding that the ordinance was not about the Council but the community, that the community had requested Council to act on it this evening, that it was the right thing to do, that there were 6.5 million single-use bags in the City, which was astronomical, and that this was a great step forward. Councilmember Roberts stated that he had met with the California Grocer's Association with the City Manager and Attorney, that the language in the ordinance was accurate, and that concerns of plastic bag use at restaurants was addressed in the ordinance.
MOTION: Moved by Heebner and seconded by Roberts.
Motion carried unanimously.

C.4.
San Onofre. (File 0230-51)
Recommendation: That the City Council
1.
Review proposed correspondence and provide direction as appropriate
David Ott, City Manager, introduced the item. He stated that over the past couple months the public had expressed concerns regarding the operational safety of the plant, that this item was heard at the last Council meeting and direction was given for Staff to prepare draft letters to send to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and various representatives on behalf of the Council, and that those letters were ready for Council review and approval.
Shawn Bernie (time donated by Torgen Johnson) from Friends of the Earth stated that he had worked on nuclear power issues for more than 30 years, that he had spent more than 20 years working in East Asia, Korean, China, and Japan, particularly working on the nuclear fuel cycle in Japan. He stated that he spent a lot of time working with communities there, that they were well informed and understood the problems of nuclear power plants in Japan. He stated that those people had been working for years to inform others of the danger of nuclear plants, that tere were 54 power reactors operating in Japan at the time of Fukushima, that today there was one operating, that the nuclear issues were ignored by officials in Japan, and that was why there was Fukushima. He stated that when he was driving down the coast, he was struck by the similarities of the reactor sites of San Clemente, that 1,450 tons of spent fuel stored at San Onofre was discharged every refueling cycle, that San Onofre was effectively stored inside a community of 65,000 people, and that it was similar to Japan. He posed the question of what would be the consequences of a San Onofre nuclear accident, that it was an accident waiting to happen, and that citizens knew that there was something wrong with how nuclear power was regulated in the United States. He stated that unless action was taken to shut down old nuclear reactors we would be talking about our own nuclear catastrophe, and that informed citizens and politicians could make the right decisions.
Arnie Gunderson (time donated by Swedina Hurt) Consultant for Friends of the Earth, stated that he was concerned about San Onofre. He showed a sketch of the reactor at San Onofre which he stated had a nuclear core of only about 12ft x 12 ft x12ft, that in the nuclear core there was 350 million horsepower being generated, that it was a u-tube steam generator, and that 200 million pounds of water a minute was being run through the nuclear steam generator. He stated that unit 2 was shut down in early January, that they knew that unit 2 had significant problems prior to the unit 3 failure, that there were 9,700 tubes in the steam generator, and that the tubes vibrated and hit each other. He stated that the one tube that failed had a pin hole leak and was leaking half-a-gallon a minute, that there was a 1,200 pound pressure difference across the tube, that the tube would have been cut by the high pressure water in less than a day, in which 1,000 gallons a minute would have leaked, and that the problem was brought on because the old steam generator should have been repaired and old materials replaced. He stated that San Onofre made a mistake, that they decided to add more tubes, that those tubes were not necessary and changed the dynamics inside the generator, that the solution for San Onofre was to plug the "u" to prevent the tube from leaking but not injuring the tube next to it, and that he was concerned that this problem would not be solved by the Summer.
Council discussion ensued with the speaker that San Onofre was trying to squeeze out more power in the future by adding the adding the additional 4% tubes, that the original specs for the plant stated how many tubes were required, that this was the biggest steam generator in the world that had been replaced, that in the old steam generator there was pillar holding the tubes up, and that in order to get an additional 400 tubes in, the pillar was removed which changed the flow and vibrations of the tubes, which was why we were here today.
Council discussion continued with the speaker regarding the proposed letter to the Nucelar Regulatory Committee (NRC), the speaker stated that the letter was accurate, that it addressed regulatory concerns, and that letters from communities were important. The speaker stated that the 2 worst sites in the country for evacuation planning were Indian Point, New York, and San Onofre, that every single Nuclear Regulatory Commissioner had been vetted by the nuclear industry before they were appointed, that a former commissioner stated that the the entire congress was pro-nuclear and were putting in pro-nuclear commissioners, and that the 50 mile radius concept came from Fukishima.
Council and the speaker discussed the safety of San Onofre, that the population around San Onofre has blossomed since it was made, that it could have been evacuated in the 1980s but not now, that there were 2 problems with San Onofre, 1) that San Onofre had significant whistle blower complaints, and led the nation for the last 6 years in those complaints, that this was indicative of a management breakdown, and that this was the biggest distinction between San Onofre and other plants. Also, that a lot had been learned regarding location of the plant since it was built, that seismic issues were more serious than we understood them to be in the 80s, and that the concrete and structures of the plant were weakening because of the salt air from the ocean.
Council requested to have a quarterly update on this issue in memorandum form to keep Council updated on the issue.
Torgen Johnson thanked the Council for due diligence, and stated that this was an important issue. He stated that the City of Irvine had voted 5/0 on it, and that they concluded that Southern California Edison had to be held responsible for the decisions they were making when they were risking our lives.
Richard Moore stated that he had submitted a letter to the Council, and that Council should not to be driven by fear of the unknown but by facts when making these decisions.
Ace Hoffman stated that the plant should never be reopened, that the spent fuel pool 4 in Fukushima was leaning and that if it fell, the amount of seeds that would be released would be 85% more than was released in Chernobyl. He stated that there was more in San onofre that could be released, that there was various ways that the waste could be released at San Onofre, that he had been speaking at various cities speaking on the topic, and that there were plenty of facts to make this decision on.
MOTION: Moved by Heebner and seconded by Campbell to approve the letter.
Motion carried unanimously.
